prompt: A dataset of a million photographs keeps only the file names in `__init__`, and its `__getitem__` opens and decodes one file. When is a photograph decoded?
hint: Which of the two methods does the loader call per item?

choices.text: All of them when the dataset object is created
choices.why: `__init__` only stored names; nothing in it opens a file.

choices.text: All of them when the `DataLoader` is built
choices.why: Building a loader reads no item; it only records how to ask for them.

choices.text: Each one when its index is asked for, at every read
choices.why: Right. `__getitem__` runs per item, so the work happens one image at a time, and again in every epoch.

choices.text: Once per epoch, the whole set at the start of it
choices.why: Nothing reads ahead by the whole set; items are asked for as batches are built.

prompt: Write the two methods a map-style PyTorch dataset defines: ___ for the number of items, and ___ for item number i.
hint: Both have two underscores on each side.

prompt: A training set has 1,000 images, and the loader uses `batch_size=64` with `drop_last=False`. How many batches does one epoch have?
hint: Fifteen full batches hold 960 images.

prompt: With `shuffle=True` and `drop_last=True`, 21 of the 1,077 training images are left out of every epoch. Which ones?
hint: When is the order decided, and how often?

choices.text: The last 21 of the dataset, by index
choices.why: That would be true with `shuffle=False`; shuffled, the last batch holds whatever the permutation put last.

choices.text: A different 21 every epoch, chosen by that epoch's shuffle
choices.why: Right. Each epoch draws a new order, and the short batch at its end is whatever landed there, so over many epochs every image is used.

choices.text: The same 21 in every epoch, the ones picked at the first shuffle
choices.why: `batches.py` showed epoch 2 starting differently from epoch 1: the shuffle is redone each time.

choices.text: None, because they move to the front of the next epoch
choices.why: The loader keeps nothing from one epoch to the next; the leftovers are dropped.

prompt: A dataset of photographs returns images of different sizes, and the loader fails inside `default_collate` saying the tensors must be equal size. What fixes it and keeps batches of 32?
hint: Which step puts 32 items into one tensor?

choices.text: `drop_last=True`
choices.why: It removes the short last batch; the full batches still mix sizes.

choices.text: `shuffle=False`, so that similar photographs are read together
choices.why: Order does not make two sizes stackable; neighbours in the files can differ just as much.

choices.text: `num_workers=0`, so one process builds every batch
choices.why: The workers call the same `default_collate`; the error is the same in the main process.

choices.text: A `collate_fn` that pads or crops each batch to one size
choices.why: Right. Collating is the step that stacks items, so a collate function that makes them one size first is where the fix belongs; a transform that resizes every image is the other place.

prompt: `ltrain.py` uses lesson 9's seeds, network, rate and batch size, yet ends at a validation accuracy of 0.956 where lesson 9 ended at 0.950. Why?
hint: What decides which images go into each batch?

choices.text: The loader converts the images to `float64`
choices.why: Collating keeps the dtype; the batches are `float32` like the tensors in `tdigits.py`.

choices.text: Its shuffles differ, so the batches differ
choices.why: Right. The loader draws from its generator in its own way, so the same seed gives other batches, and the run lands near lesson 9's rather than on it.

choices.text: The loader drops the last short batch unless told not to
choices.why: `drop_last` is `False` by default, and `batches.py` counted 34 batches with a last one of 21.

choices.text: `loop.evaluate` measures differently on data that came through a loader
choices.why: The validation set does not go through the loader at all; it is the same tensors as in lesson 9.

prompt: `warped[0]` read twice gave two different images. What does that mean for a training run of 30 epochs?
hint: When does the transform run?

choices.text: A new variant of every digit in every epoch
choices.why: Right. The transform runs at each read, so each epoch draws fresh fields, which is what augmentation is for.

choices.text: The labels change with the image, so they must be recomputed
choices.why: The label comes from `self.y[i]` untouched; only the image goes through the transform.

choices.text: The dataset grows to 30 stored copies of each image
choices.why: Nothing is stored; each variant exists only until its batch has been used.

choices.text: Validation accuracy can be compared only between runs with equal fields
choices.why: The validation set is read without the transform, so its images are the same in every run.

prompt: To save time, someone runs `Warp` once over the training set in `__init__` and stores the 1,077 results. What does the training lose?
hint: How many different versions of a digit does each approach show the network?

choices.text: Nothing, as the network sees warped digits either way
choices.why: It sees one fixed warp of each digit, every epoch, instead of a new one each time.

choices.text: Its labels, which `__init__` cannot reach
choices.why: `__init__` holds the labels already; they are untouched by the transform.

choices.text: Variety: every epoch repeats the same images
choices.why: Right. Precomputing turns a random transform into a fixed one, which is cheaper and no longer augments; only a part with no randomness in it, like a fixed resize, can be cached without loss.

choices.text: The noise, which `torch.randn` refuses to draw in `__init__`
choices.why: `torch.randn` works anywhere; the noise would be drawn once and frozen, like the rest.

prompt: `workers.py` has no model in it at all. What does its time per epoch tell you about a training run with the same loader?
hint: Can a training epoch take less time than reading its batches?

choices.text: Nothing, because a model changes how fast the loader reads its items
choices.why: The model shares the processors and can slow the loader down, but it cannot make reading faster.

choices.text: The shortest that training epoch can be, whatever the model costs
choices.why: Right. Every batch has to be built before it is used, so the loader's own epoch is a floor that a faster model or a graphics card cannot go below.

choices.text: How long the model's forward pass takes per batch
choices.why: There is no forward pass in it; each batch is taken and thrown away.

choices.text: The time training takes, since the model's share of it is negligible
choices.why: That holds only when computing is small; `waiting.py` shows the two parts measured apart.

prompt: Four transforms each add random noise and run in a loader with four workers. Which one gives the same noise in every worker?
hint: PyTorch seeds some generators in each worker as it starts. Which generator was made before the workers existed?

choices.text: One calling `torch.randn` on every read
choices.why: Each worker's torch generator is seeded differently, which is why `Warp` needed no fixing.

choices.text: One calling Python's `random.gauss`
choices.why: PyTorch also seeds Python's `random` module in each worker.

choices.text: One calling the global `np.random.normal` on every read
choices.why: NumPy's global generator is seeded per worker by PyTorch; only a generator object of your own is copied unchanged.

choices.text: One drawing from `np.random.default_rng(0)` stored by `__init__`
choices.why: Right. That generator object is copied into each worker as it was, so they all draw the same numbers, as `twins.py` showed; a `worker_init_fn` has to replace it.

prompt: Match each `DataLoader` argument to what it does.
hint: One description belongs to no argument here.

pairs.right: how many extra processes build batches
keeps those processes alive between epochs
puts batches in page-locked memory for copies to a card
throws away the short batch at the end

right_distractors: how many images go into one batch

prompt: A transform costs 2 ms per image, batches hold 64 images, there are no workers, and a graphics card does each training step in 5 ms. For what percentage of the epoch does the card sit idle?
hint: Building one batch takes 64 × 2 ms, and nothing else happens meanwhile.

prompt: `nvidia-smi` shows the card at 35% utilisation during training. What is the first thing to measure?
hint: Before changing anything, find out what the other 65% is.

choices.text: Waiting time against computing time, per batch
choices.why: Right. Low utilisation says the card is often idle, not why; splitting the time as `waiting.py` does says whether the loader is the cause.

choices.text: Whether a larger model would keep the card busier
choices.why: A larger model raises the percentage by making each step longer, and the run gets slower, not faster.

choices.text: The card's temperature under that load
choices.why: A hot card slows its own computing; it does not leave it idle two thirds of the time.

choices.text: The learning rate's effect on the loss
choices.why: The rate decides what a step does to the weights, not how long the card waits for one.

prompt: Two workers brought the wait per batch down on this machine. The same loader then feeds a card that computes 30 times faster. What happens to the wait per batch?
hint: While the step ran, the workers were building the next batch. How long is the step now?

choices.text: It stays the same, as the workers have not changed
choices.why: The wait depends on how much of the building happens behind the step, and the step got shorter.

choices.text: It grows: a shorter step hides less of the building
choices.why: Right. The workers need about as long as before to build a batch; with less computing to overlap, more of that time shows up as waiting.

choices.text: It falls to zero, because the card copies the data itself
choices.why: The card copies batches that exist; building them is still the processor's work.

choices.text: It falls by 30 times, like the computing does
choices.why: Computing and loading run on different hardware; speeding one up does nothing to the other.

prompt: In a training loop, `xb.to(device)` sits on a line of its own, with nothing assigned. What happens to `xb` on a machine with a card?
hint: Compare the tensor and the module in `todevice.py`.

choices.text: It moves to the card, as a module does
choices.why: A module changes itself; a tensor's `.to` returns a new tensor and leaves the old one where it was.

choices.text: It stays where it was; the copy is lost
choices.why: Right. The next line then feeds a processor tensor to a model on the card, and PyTorch stops with a device error.

choices.text: It is moved later, at the moment the model first reads it
choices.why: PyTorch moves nothing on its own; a mismatch is an error, not a silent copy.

choices.text: It is moved and pinned, since the loader pinned it
choices.why: Pinning prepares a copy; it does not make an unassigned `.to` take effect.

prompt: What did `pin_memory=True` do on the lab machine, which has no graphics card?
hint: Look at the line the one-line program printed after the warning.

choices.text: It made every batch faster to read from memory
choices.why: Pinned memory speeds up copies to a card, and there is no card here to copy to.

choices.text: It stopped the program with an error
choices.why: The program ran on and printed its line; the complaint was a warning.

choices.text: It pinned the batch in the processor's memory for later
choices.why: `is_pinned()` answered `False`: nothing was pinned.

choices.text: Nothing, after a warning
choices.why: Right. With no accelerator, PyTorch warns and skips pinning, which is why `todevice.py` asks for it only when the device is `cuda`.

prompt: A loop copies a batch with `xb.to('cuda', non_blocking=True)` and calls `model(xb)` on the next line. Can the model read a half-copied batch?
hint: Who is it that does not wait: the processor or the card?

choices.text: No: the card runs the copy and then the model, in order
choices.why: Right. The processor goes on without waiting, but the card queues the copy before the model's operations, so they read a complete batch.

choices.text: Yes, and the loss comes out wrong for that batch
choices.why: Work on one stream of the card runs in the order it was queued, so the copy finishes first.

choices.text: No, because `non_blocking` is ignored for model inputs
choices.why: It is not ignored; it lets the processor go on while the copy runs.

choices.text: Yes, unless `torch.cuda.synchronize()` is called first
choices.why: Synchronising makes the processor wait for the card; the card was already keeping its own order.

prompt: An epoch spends 80% of its time waiting for data. Which changes shorten it? Choose every one that does.
hint: Which side of the time does each change act on?

choices.text: More workers, while processors are free
choices.why: Right: batches are built in parallel and behind the step.

choices.text: Caching the part of the transform with no randomness
choices.why: Right: work done once is not repeated at every read.

choices.text: A graphics card twice as fast
choices.why: It shortens the 20% spent computing and leaves the 80% as it was.

choices.text: `non_blocking=True` on a machine without a card
choices.why: On the processor there is no copy to overlap, so nothing changes.

prompt: Put in order what happens for one batch of a loader with no workers, up to the forward pass.
hint: Indices come before items.
items: The sampler picks 32 indices from the shuffled order
`__getitem__` runs once for each index, transform included
The collate function stacks the 32 items into one batch
The batch is moved to the device
The model runs its forward pass on the batch

prompt: On a laptop with four processors, a loader with `num_workers=8` and a CPU-trained model is slower than with `num_workers=3`. What explains it?
hint: What else needs those four processors?

choices.text: Each worker reads the whole dataset, so eight read it eight times
choices.why: The workers split the batches between them; each item of an epoch is read once.

choices.text: Too many processes for four processors
choices.why: Right. Past the number of free processors, extra workers only take turns, and they take turns with the model's own computing too.

choices.text: `num_workers` above the batch size wastes workers
choices.why: Workers build whole batches, one each; the batch size does not cap them.

choices.text: Eight workers turn shuffling off
choices.why: Shuffling is decided by the sampler in the main process, whatever the number of workers.
